youtube.title: HOT TUB
youtube.summary: Rodney Hide and Paul Brennan discuss growing social disconnection, the erosion of empathy and duty, and the lasting impact of the COVID years. They examine the US midterm results, political tribalism and media bias before turning to New Zealand’s election. Drawing on Hide’s successful 2005 Epsom campaign, they explain how the overhang strategy can make votes count more effectively and explain how it could help deliver a centre-right victory. youtube.title: GRAEME EDGELER
youtube.summary: Talking with Paul Brennan, lawyer Graeme Edgeler examines the unusual veto provision in The Opportunity Party’s rules and whether two board members could block a coalition agreement after the election. He explains why elected MPs ultimately hold the power to make decisions in Parliament, how a disagreement could complicate negotiations and why TOP may need to rethink its internal structures if it enters Parliament for the first time. youtube.title: MAREWA GLOVER
youtube.summary: Talking with Maree Buscke, Dr Marewa Glover challenges the idea that Māori society was traditionally socialist, arguing that tribal structures, identity and resource allocation have been reshaped by modern political ideology. She examines the growing influence of urban Māori organisations, the politics of identity and Treaty interpretation and the impact of Covid-era brainwashing and it impact on public health policies. Discover more from Marewa on X

youtube.title: NICOLE MCKEE
youtube.summary: Talking with Maree Buscke, ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee outlines the party’s plans to strengthen law and order, including a proposed three-strikes regime for repeat burglars, tougher penalties for rural crime and expanded powers for accredited security guards. She also discusses making better use of healthcare funding by giving pharmacists a greater role, reducing government bureaucracy, improving ministerial accountability and navigating the coalition negotiations that may follow the election. youtube.summary: Australia’s housing market is facing a potentially historic downturn, with the Commonwealth Bank forecasting a 14% fall in dwelling prices from peak to trough. Michael Arbon examines the factors behind the decline, including rising interest rates, stretched affordability and government policies that have encouraged high-risk borrowing.
